Job 1.summary: Job of Uz is "perfect and upright," with seven sons, three daughters, and great wealth, and he offers sacrifices for his children (Job 1:1–5). When the sons of God come before the LORD, Satan asks, "Doth Job fear God for nought?" and the LORD lets him touch all that Job has, but not Job himself (Job 1:6–12). In one day messengers report that Job's oxen, sheep, camels, servants, and all his children are gone (Job 1:13–19). Job tears his mantle, worships, and says, "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD" (Job 1:20–22).
Job 1.whereWeAre: Esther ended the history books with Mordecai honored in Persia. Job begins the books of poetry with a man in the land of Uz, "perfect and upright" (Job 1:1), who loses his wealth and all ten children in one day yet blesses the LORD. In chapter 2 Satan is allowed to strike Job's body.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: A man of Uz who loses everything and still blesses the LORD.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Points to Job's integrity and lets Satan test him.

keyFigures.name: Satan
keyFigures.role: Claims Job serves God only for what he gets.

keyFigures.name: The messengers
keyFigures.role: Bring Job four reports of disaster in one day.

keyThemes.explanation: Satan claims Job serves God only for blessings, and the test will show otherwise.
Job blesses the LORD's name after losing everything.
Satan can go only as far as the LORD allows.

Job 2.summary: Satan comes before the LORD again, and the LORD lets him strike Job's body but spare his life (Job 2:1–6). Satan covers Job with boils, and Job sits among the ashes and scrapes himself with a potsherd (Job 2:7–8). His wife says, "curse God, and die," but Job answers, "shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?" (Job 2:9–10). Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar come to comfort him and sit with him seven days and nights without a word (Job 2:11–13).
Job 2.whereWeAre: Job lost his wealth and children in chapter 1 without sinning. Now Satan strikes him with boils, his wife tells him to curse God, and three friends come and sit with him in silence for seven days. In chapter 3 Job finally speaks.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Struck with boils, yet does not sin with his lips.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Lets Satan strike Job's body but spare his life.

keyFigures.name: Satan
keyFigures.role: Covers Job with sore boils.

keyFigures.name: Job's wife
keyFigures.role: Tells Job, "curse God, and die."

keyFigures.name: Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar
keyFigures.role: Job's friends, who come to comfort him and sit in silence.

keyThemes.explanation: Job holds to his integrity even when his own body is struck.

keyThemes.theme: Good and evil from God's hand
keyThemes.explanation: Job accepts trouble as well as blessing from God.
The friends' best comfort is seven days of sitting with Job in silence.

Job 3.summary: Job breaks his silence and curses the day he was born: "Let the day perish wherein I was born" (Job 3:1–10). He asks why he did not die at birth, where he would now be at rest with kings and prisoners alike (Job 3:11–19). He asks why light is given to those who long for death, and says, "the thing which I greatly feared is come upon me" (Job 3:20–26).
Job 3.whereWeAre: Job's friends sat with him seven days in silence at the end of chapter 2. Now Job curses the day he was born and asks why the suffering are kept alive. In chapter 4 Eliphaz begins the first round of speeches.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Curses the day of his birth and asks why he still lives.

keyThemes.explanation: Job pours out his pain without hiding it.
Job pictures the grave as a place where the weary rest.
Job asks why life is given to those who long for death.

Job 4.summary: Eliphaz the Temanite reminds Job that his words once strengthened others, but now he faints when trouble comes to him (Job 4:1–6). He asks, "who ever perished, being innocent?" and says those who sow wickedness reap the same (Job 4:7–11). He tells of a spirit in the night that asked, "Shall mortal man be more just than God?" (Job 4:12–21).
Job 4.whereWeAre: Job cursed the day of his birth in chapter 3. Now Eliphaz, the first friend to speak, reminds Job that "who ever perished, being innocent?" (Job 4:7) and tells of a vision in the night. He continues in chapter 5.

keyFigures.name: Eliphaz
keyFigures.role: The Temanite, who says the innocent do not perish and tells of a night vision.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: The one Eliphaz is answering.

keyThemes.explanation: Eliphaz believes suffering always comes from sin.
Mortal man cannot be more just than God.
Eliphaz's words, though partly true, do not fit Job's case.

Job 5.summary: Eliphaz says wrath kills the foolish and that "man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward" (Job 5:1–7). He tells Job to seek God, who does great things and saves the poor (Job 5:8–16). He says, "happy is the man whom God correcteth," and promises Job safety, children, and long life if he accepts it (Job 5:17–27).
Job 5.whereWeAre: Eliphaz began his speech in chapter 4. Here he tells Job to seek God and accept his correction, promising that God will restore him. In chapter 6 Job answers that his friends have failed him.

keyFigures.name: Eliphaz
keyFigures.role: Tells Job to seek God and accept his correction.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: The one Eliphaz is answering.

keyThemes.explanation: Eliphaz says trouble is as natural as sparks flying upward.
God saves the poor and brings down the crafty.
Eliphaz says the man God corrects is happy, if he accepts it.

explainedReferences.explanation: Catching the wise in their craftiness.

Job 6.summary: Job answers that his grief would be heavier than the sand of the sea, for "the arrows of the Almighty are within me" (Job 6:1–7). He wishes God would cut him off (Job 6:8–13). He says his friends have failed him like streams that vanish in the heat (Job 6:14–23). He asks them to show him where he has gone wrong (Job 6:24–30).
Job 6.whereWeAre: Eliphaz told Job to accept God's correction in chapters 4–5. Job answers that his grief is heavier than the sand and that his friends are like streams that dry up. In chapter 7 he turns from them to speak to God.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Says his grief is heavy and his friends have failed him.

keyThemes.explanation: Job's pain is too heavy to measure.
Job's friends are like streams that dry up when needed.
Job asks to be shown his error instead of being accused.

Job 7.summary: Job says his life is like the hard days of a hired servant, with nights of tossing and flesh covered with worms (Job 7:1–5). "My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle," he says, and he will not keep silent (Job 7:6–11). He asks God why he frightens him with dreams and will not let him alone (Job 7:12–19). He ends, "why dost thou not pardon my transgression?" (Job 7:20–21).
Job 7.whereWeAre: Job told his friends they had failed him in chapter 6. Now he speaks to God about how short and hard life is and asks why God will not leave him alone. In chapter 8 Bildad answers.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Speaks to God about the shortness and pain of life.

keyThemes.explanation: Job says his days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle.
Job will not hold back the anguish of his spirit.
Job asks why God pays such close attention to man.

Job 8.summary: Bildad the Shuhite asks, "Doth God pervert judgment?" and says Job's children were cast away for their sin (Job 8:1–4). If Job is pure and seeks God, God will restore him (Job 8:5–7). Bildad tells Job to learn from the fathers that those who forget God wither like reeds without water (Job 8:8–19). God will not cast away a perfect man, he says, and will yet fill Job's mouth with laughing (Job 8:20–22).
Job 8.whereWeAre: Job asked God why he would not pardon him in chapter 7. Now Bildad asks, "Doth God pervert judgment?" (Job 8:3) and says Job's children died for their sin. In chapter 9 Job answers.

keyFigures.name: Bildad
keyFigures.role: The Shuhite, who says God never perverts justice.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: The one Bildad is answering.

keyThemes.explanation: Bildad insists that God never perverts judgment.
Bildad appeals to what earlier generations taught.
Those who forget God wither like reeds without water.

Job 9.summary: Job asks, "how should man be just with God?" for God moves mountains and made Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades (Job 9:1–13). Even if he were righteous, Job says, he could not answer God (Job 9:14–21). He says God destroys the perfect and the wicked alike, and his days flee away (Job 9:22–31). He wishes there were "any daysman betwixt us," someone to stand between him and God (Job 9:32–35).
Job 9.whereWeAre: Bildad insisted in chapter 8 that God never perverts justice. Job agrees that no one can win an argument with God and wishes for a "daysman" to stand between them. He keeps speaking to God in chapter 10.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Says no one can argue with God and wishes for a daysman.

keyThemes.explanation: God moves mountains and made the stars.
Job feels he cannot be justified in God's court.
Job longs for a daysman to stand between him and God.

Job 10.summary: Job says, "My soul is weary of my life," and asks God to show him why he contends with him (Job 10:1–7). He reminds God, "Thine hands have made me and fashioned me," and asks why God would now destroy him (Job 10:8–17). He asks why he was born and begs for a little comfort before he goes to the land of darkness (Job 10:18–22).
Job 10.whereWeAre: Job wished for someone to judge between him and God in chapter 9. Now he asks God why he would destroy the one his own hands made. In chapter 11 Zophar answers sharply.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Asks God why he would destroy what his hands have made.

keyThemes.explanation: Job reminds God that his hands shaped him.
Job asks God to show why he is contending with him.
Job asks for a little comfort before he dies.

Job 11.summary: Zophar the Naamathite says Job's many words should not go unanswered, and that God exacts less than his iniquity deserves (Job 11:1–6). He asks, "Canst thou by searching find out God?" (Job 11:7–12). If Job puts away his sin, Zophar says, he will forget his misery and live in safety (Job 11:13–20).
Job 11.whereWeAre: Job pleaded with his Maker in chapter 10. Now Zophar, the third friend, says Job deserves even more than he suffers and calls him to put away his sin. Job answers in chapters 12–14.

keyFigures.name: Zophar
keyFigures.role: The Naamathite, who tells Job he deserves worse and must repent.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: The one Zophar is answering.

keyThemes.explanation: No one can find out God by searching.
Zophar says Job deserves even more than he suffers.
If Job puts away sin, Zophar says, he will be secure.

Job 12.summary: Job answers, "No doubt but ye are the people, and wisdom shall die with you," and says he understands as much as they do (Job 12:1–6). He says even the beasts and the earth know that the LORD's hand has made all things (Job 12:7–12). God has wisdom and strength, and he brings down counsellors, judges, kings, and priests (Job 12:13–25).
Job 12.whereWeAre: Zophar told Job to repent in chapter 11. Job answers with scorn for his friends' wisdom and describes God's power over nature and kings. He continues in chapter 13.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Mocks his friends' wisdom and describes God's power.

keyThemes.explanation: The beasts and the earth know that God made them.
God brings down counsellors, judges, and kings.
Job mocks his friends for thinking they alone are wise.

Job 13.summary: Job says he wants to speak to the Almighty, and calls his friends "forgers of lies" (Job 13:1–5). He asks whether they will speak wickedly for God (Job 13:6–12). He says, "Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him," and declares that he has ordered his cause (Job 13:13–19). He asks God to show him his sins and asks why God hides his face (Job 13:20–28).
Job 13.whereWeAre: Job mocked his friends' wisdom in chapter 12. Now he tells them they speak lies for God and declares, "Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him" (Job 13:15). Chapter 14 ends his first answer to Zophar.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Calls his friends forgers of lies and asks to plead his case with God.

keyThemes.explanation: Job warns his friends not to lie in God's defense.
Job will trust God even if God slays him.
Job asks God to tell him his sins.

Job 14.summary: Job says, "Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble" (Job 14:1–6). A tree that is cut down may sprout again, but man dies and does not rise (Job 14:7–12). He asks, "If a man die, shall he live again?" and longs to be hidden until God's wrath is past (Job 14:13–17). As water wears away stones, he says, God destroys the hope of man (Job 14:18–22).
Job 14.whereWeAre: Job asked God to show him his sins in chapter 13. Now he mourns that man is "of few days, and full of trouble" (Job 14:1) and asks, "If a man die, shall he live again?" (Job 14:14). In chapter 15 Eliphaz opens the second round.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Mourns that man's life is short and asks if the dead live again.

keyThemes.explanation: Human life is short and full of trouble.
A cut tree may sprout again, but man seems to have no such hope.
Job asks whether the dead will live again.

Job 15.summary: Eliphaz opens the second round, saying Job's own mouth condemns him (Job 15:1–6). He asks whether Job is wiser than the old men who are with them (Job 15:7–16). He describes the wicked man who lives in fear and darkness all his days (Job 15:17–35).
Job 15.whereWeAre: The first round of speeches ended with chapter 14. Now Eliphaz accuses Job of empty talk and describes the terrors of the wicked. In chapter 16 Job answers.

keyFigures.name: Eliphaz
keyFigures.role: Says Job's own words condemn him.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: The one Eliphaz is answering.

keyThemes.explanation: Eliphaz says Job's own mouth condemns him.
Eliphaz appeals to the gray-haired men among them.
The wicked live in constant fear.

Job 16.summary: Job answers, "miserable comforters are ye all," and says he would comfort them if they were in his place (Job 16:1–5). He says God has worn him out and broken him (Job 16:6–17). Yet he says, "my witness is in heaven," and he weeps to God (Job 16:18–22).
Job 16.whereWeAre: Eliphaz described the fate of the wicked in chapter 15. Job calls his friends "miserable comforters" (Job 16:2) and says his witness is in heaven. He continues in chapter 17.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Calls his friends miserable comforters and looks to his witness in heaven.

keyThemes.explanation: Job says his friends' words only add to his pain.
Job describes God as tearing and breaking him.
Job hopes for someone in heaven to plead for him.

Job 17.summary: Job says his breath is corrupt and the graves are ready for him, and mockers surround him (Job 17:1–2). He asks God to be his surety, for he has become a byword (Job 17:3–9). "My days are past," he says, and asks, "where is now my hope?" (Job 17:10–16).
Job 17.whereWeAre: Job looked for a witness in heaven in chapter 16. Now he says his spirit is broken and the grave is waiting for him. In chapter 18 Bildad answers.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Says his spirit is broken and his hope is gone.

keyThemes.explanation: Job says his days are ended and the grave is ready.
Job has become a byword among the people.
The righteous will hold on to their way.

Job 18.summary: Bildad asks how long Job will go on and why the friends are counted as beasts (Job 18:1–4). He says the light of the wicked shall be put out, and traps catch his feet (Job 18:5–10). Terrors chase the wicked, and "His remembrance shall perish from the earth" (Job 18:11–21).
Job 18.whereWeAre: Job said in chapter 17 that his hope was gone. Now Bildad describes how the light of the wicked is put out and their name is forgotten. In chapter 19 Job answers with his great statement of hope.

keyFigures.name: Bildad
keyFigures.role: Describes the terrible end of the wicked.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: The one Bildad is answering.

keyThemes.explanation: Bildad says the light of the wicked will be put out.
The wicked are caught in their own nets.
The wicked leave no name or children behind.

Job 19.summary: Job asks, "How long will ye vex my soul?" and says God has fenced up his way (Job 19:1–12). His brothers, friends, servants, and even his wife have turned from him (Job 19:13–22). He wishes his words were cut in rock and says, "For I know that my redeemer liveth" (Job 19:23–27). He warns his friends to fear the sword of judgment (Job 19:28–29).
Job 19.whereWeAre: Bildad described the end of the wicked in chapter 18. Job says everyone has turned against him, yet declares, "I know that my redeemer liveth" (Job 19:25). In chapter 20 Zophar answers.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Feels abandoned by all, yet says, "I know that my redeemer liveth."

keyThemes.explanation: Job's family and friends have all turned away from him.
Job wishes his words were carved in stone.
Job is sure that his redeemer lives and that he will see God.

Job 20.summary: Zophar says "the triumphing of the wicked is short" (Job 20:1–11). Though wickedness is sweet in his mouth, it turns to the poison of asps inside him (Job 20:12–22). God's wrath falls on him, and "This is the portion of a wicked man from God" (Job 20:23–29).
Job 20.whereWeAre: Job spoke of his redeemer in chapter 19. Now Zophar says the joy of the wicked is short and their riches turn to poison. In chapter 21 Job answers that the wicked often prosper.

keyFigures.name: Zophar
keyFigures.role: Says the joy of the wicked is short.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: The one Zophar is answering.

keyThemes.explanation: Zophar says the joy of the wicked lasts only a moment.
Wickedness tastes sweet but turns to poison.
Zophar says God's wrath is the wicked man's portion.

Job 21.summary: Job asks his friends to listen to him, then let them mock (Job 21:1–6). He asks, "Wherefore do the wicked live, become old, yea, are mighty in power?" (Job 21:7–16). Their houses are safe and their children dance, though they tell God, "Depart from us" (Job 21:9–15). One man dies at ease and another in bitterness, and both lie in the dust (Job 21:17–26). Job says his friends' answers are false comfort (Job 21:27–34).
Job 21.whereWeAre: Zophar claimed in chapter 20 that the wicked soon fall. Job answers that many wicked people live long, grow rich, and die in peace. In chapter 22 Eliphaz opens the third round.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Says the wicked often prosper and die in peace.

keyThemes.explanation: Job points out that many wicked people live long and well.
The prosperous wicked tell God to depart from them.
The happy and the bitter both lie down in the dust.

Job 22.summary: Eliphaz asks, "Is not thy wickedness great?" (Job 22:1–5). He accuses Job of taking pledges, withholding bread and water, and sending widows away empty (Job 22:6–11). He says Job thinks God cannot see through the clouds (Job 22:12–20). He urges, "Acquaint now thyself with him, and be at peace" (Job 22:21–30).
Job 22.whereWeAre: Job ended the second round in chapter 21. Now Eliphaz accuses Job of specific sins against the poor and urges him to return to God. In chapter 23 Job answers.

keyFigures.name: Eliphaz
keyFigures.role: Accuses Job of cruelty to the poor and urges him to return to God.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: The one Eliphaz is accusing.

keyThemes.explanation: Eliphaz accuses Job of sins Job never committed.
Eliphaz says God is not blind behind the clouds.
Eliphaz urges Job to make peace with God.

Job 23.summary: Job says, "Oh that I knew where I might find him!" and longs to lay his case before God (Job 23:1–7). He cannot find God anywhere, "But he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold" (Job 23:8–12). He is troubled at God's presence, for God does what he wills (Job 23:13–17).
Job 23.whereWeAre: Eliphaz accused Job of cruelty in chapter 22. Job longs to find God and plead his case, sure that "when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold" (Job 23:10). He continues in chapter 24.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Longs to find God and believes he will come forth as gold.

keyThemes.explanation: Job longs to find God and lay his case before him.
Job believes testing will prove him true.
Job values God's words more than his daily food.

Job 24.summary: Job asks why the wicked are not judged, as some move landmarks and take the flocks of the fatherless (Job 24:1–4). The poor go naked, hungry, and wet with rain while they work for others (Job 24:5–12). Murderers, adulterers, and thieves work in the dark (Job 24:13–17). Job says they are lifted up for a little while and then brought low (Job 24:18–25).
Job 24.whereWeAre: Job longed to find God in chapter 23. Now he describes how the poor are robbed and the wicked seem to go unpunished. In chapter 25 Bildad gives his last, short speech.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Describes how the poor are oppressed while the wicked go free.

keyThemes.explanation: The wicked rob the needy and the fatherless.
Murderers and thieves hide their work in darkness.
Job asks why God seems slow to judge the wicked.

Job 25.summary: Bildad says, "Dominion and fear are with him" (Job 25:1–3). He asks, "How then can man be justified with God?" for even the moon and stars are not pure in his sight, "How much less man, that is a worm?" (Job 25:4–6).
Job 25.whereWeAre: Job described the suffering of the poor in chapter 24. Bildad's short speech asks how any man can be clean before God. It is the friends' last word, and Job answers in chapter 26.

keyFigures.name: Bildad
keyFigures.role: Asks how any man can be righteous before God.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: The one Bildad is answering.

keyThemes.explanation: Dominion and fear belong to God.
Bildad asks how anyone born of a woman can be clean before God.
Bildad compares man to a worm.

Job 26.summary: Job asks how Bildad has helped the one who has no power (Job 26:1–4). He describes God's power: he "hangeth the earth upon nothing," binds the waters in clouds, and divides the sea (Job 26:5–13). Yet "these are parts of his ways" — only a whisper of his power (Job 26:14).
Job 26.whereWeAre: Bildad's short speech in chapter 25 was the friends' last. Job answers with a picture of God's power over the heavens and the deep. He continues his closing words in chapter 27.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Answers Bildad and describes God's power over creation.

keyThemes.explanation: Job says Bildad's words have not helped him.
God hangs the earth on nothing and rules the waters.
What we see of God is only a small part of his ways.

Job 27.summary: Job swears, "As God liveth," that he will not speak wickedness and will hold fast his righteousness (Job 27:1–6). He asks what hope the hypocrite has when God takes away his soul (Job 27:7–12). He describes "the portion of a wicked man with God": his children die, his silver goes to the just, and the east wind carries him away (Job 27:13–23).
Job 27.whereWeAre: Job described God's power in chapter 26. Now he swears he will hold on to his integrity as long as he lives and describes what the wicked receive from God. Chapter 28 asks where wisdom can be found.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Swears he will hold fast his integrity.

keyThemes.explanation: Job will not give up his integrity until he dies.
The godless have no hope when God takes their life.
The wicked man's silver goes to the just.

Job 28.summary: Men dig deep into the earth for silver, gold, iron, and precious stones (Job 28:1–11). "But where shall wisdom be found?" It is not in the deep or the sea, and it cannot be bought with gold (Job 28:12–22). God alone knows its place, and he says to man, "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding" (Job 28:23–28).
Job 28.whereWeAre: Job held to his integrity in chapter 27. This chapter describes men mining deep for silver and gold but finding no mine for wisdom, which comes only from "the fear of the Lord" (Job 28:28). In chapter 29 Job remembers his past.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Continues speaking, asking where wisdom can be found.

keyThemes.explanation: Men can dig deep into the earth for treasure.
No gold or jewel can buy wisdom.
True wisdom is to fear the Lord and depart from evil.

Job 29.summary: Job says, "Oh that I were as in months past," when God watched over him and his children were around him (Job 29:1–6). When he went to the city gate, young men hid and princes stopped talking (Job 29:7–11). He helped the poor and the fatherless and says, "I was eyes to the blind, and feet was I to the lame" (Job 29:12–17). Men waited for his words, and he sat as a chief among them (Job 29:18–25).
Job 29.whereWeAre: Chapter 28 showed that wisdom is found only with God. Now Job remembers the days when he was honored at the city gate and helped the poor. Chapter 30 describes how everything has changed.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Remembers the honor and goodness of his former life.

keyThemes.explanation: Job remembers when God watched over him.
Young and old once respected Job.
Job was eyes to the blind and a father to the poor.

Job 30.summary: Now men younger than Job, whose fathers he would not have set with his dogs, mock him (Job 30:1–15). His soul is poured out, his bones ache at night, and God has cast him into the mire (Job 30:16–19). "I cry unto thee, and thou dost not hear me," he says (Job 30:20–23). He wept for the poor, but when he looked for good, evil came, and his harp turned to mourning (Job 30:24–31).
Job 30.whereWeAre: Job remembered his past honor in chapter 29. Now he describes the shame of being mocked even by outcasts, and his cries to God that go unanswered. In chapter 31 he makes his final oath of innocence.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Describes being mocked and cries to God with no answer.

keyThemes.explanation: Job is now mocked even by outcasts.
Job cries to God but feels unheard.
Job's music has turned to weeping.

Job 31.summary: Job says, "I made a covenant with mine eyes," and denies lust and deceit (Job 31:1–12). He has not ignored his servants, the poor, the widow, or the fatherless (Job 31:13–23). He has not trusted in gold, worshiped the sun or moon, or rejoiced when his enemy fell (Job 31:24–34). He cries, "Oh that one would hear me!" and "The words of Job are ended" (Job 31:35–40).
Job 31.whereWeAre: Job described his present misery in chapter 30. Now he swears he has not lusted, lied, mistreated his servants, ignored the poor, or worshiped the sun. "The words of Job are ended" (Job 31:40), and in chapter 32 a young man named Elihu speaks.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Swears an oath of innocence and asks God to answer him.

keyThemes.explanation: Job made a covenant with his eyes.
Job did not ignore the rights of his servants or the poor.
Job did not make gold his hope.
Job longs for God to answer him.

Job 32.summary: The three friends stop answering Job, "because he was righteous in his own eyes" (Job 32:1). Elihu the son of Barachel is angry with Job for justifying himself rather than God, and with the friends for finding no answer (Job 32:2–5). He says he waited because he was young, but "Great men are not always wise" (Job 32:6–10). He says he is full of words and must speak without flattering anyone (Job 32:11–22).
Job 32.whereWeAre: Job's words ended in chapter 31, and the friends have nothing more to say. Now Elihu, a younger man, speaks up, angry at both Job and the friends. In chapter 33 he speaks to Job directly.

keyFigures.name: Elihu
keyFigures.role: The son of Barachel, a young man angry with Job and the friends.

keyFigures.name: Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar
keyFigures.role: Stop answering Job.

keyThemes.explanation: Elihu is angry with Job and with the friends.

keyThemes.theme: Wisdom is not only for the old
keyThemes.explanation: Elihu says the Spirit gives understanding, not age alone.
Elihu promises to speak honestly to everyone.

Job 33.summary: Elihu asks Job to listen, saying, "The Spirit of God hath made me" (Job 33:1–7). He quotes Job's claims to be clean and says, "in this thou art not just" (Job 33:8–13). God speaks in dreams and through pain to keep a man from the pit (Job 33:14–22). If a messenger speaks for him, God says, "Deliver him from going down to the pit: I have found a ransom" (Job 33:23–30). Elihu asks Job to answer or hold his peace (Job 33:31–33).
Job 33.whereWeAre: Elihu explained in chapter 32 why he had waited to speak. Now he tells Job that God speaks through dreams and through pain to turn people back from death. In chapter 34 he defends God's justice.

keyFigures.name: Elihu
keyFigures.role: Tells Job that God speaks through dreams and pain.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: The one Elihu is answering.

keyThemes.explanation: God speaks once or twice, though people do not notice.
Elihu says God uses pain to turn people from pride.
God delivers the one for whom a ransom is found.

Job 34.summary: Elihu calls on the wise men to hear him and says Job claims to be righteous (Job 34:1–9). He says, "Yea, surely God will not do wickedly, neither will the Almighty pervert judgment" (Job 34:10–15). God shows no partiality to princes, and his eyes see every step a man takes (Job 34:16–30). Elihu says, "Job hath spoken without knowledge" (Job 34:31–37).
Job 34.whereWeAre: Elihu told Job in chapter 33 that God warns people through suffering. Now he insists that "God will not do wickedly" (Job 34:12) and says Job has spoken without knowledge. He continues in chapter 35.

keyFigures.name: Elihu
keyFigures.role: Defends God's justice and says Job spoke without knowledge.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: The one Elihu is answering.

keyThemes.explanation: Elihu insists the Almighty will not pervert judgment.
No darkness can hide the wicked from God.
Elihu says Job's words lack wisdom.

Job 35.summary: Elihu asks what advantage Job thinks there is in being righteous (Job 35:1–4). He tells Job to look at the heavens and says his sin or righteousness does not change God (Job 35:5–8). The oppressed cry out, but none says, "Where is God my maker, who giveth songs in the night?" (Job 35:9–13). He says Job opens his mouth in vain (Job 35:14–16).
Job 35.whereWeAre: Elihu defended God's justice in chapter 34. Now he says that a person's sin or righteousness does not change God, and that Job's words are empty. Chapter 36 begins Elihu's last speech.

keyFigures.name: Elihu
keyFigures.role: Says Job's righteousness does not change God.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: The one Elihu is answering.

keyThemes.explanation: Man's sin or righteousness does not change God.
God gives songs in the night to those who seek him.
Elihu says Job multiplies words without knowledge.

Job 36.summary: Elihu says he will speak on God's behalf (Job 36:1–4). God is mighty and despises no one; he opens the ears of the afflicted to correction (Job 36:5–15). Elihu warns Job not to turn to wickedness (Job 36:16–21). "Behold, God is great, and we know him not," he says, and describes the rain and the clouds (Job 36:22–33).
Job 36.whereWeAre: Elihu called Job's words empty in chapter 35. Now he says God uses affliction to open people's ears and points to God's greatness in the rain and clouds. He finishes in chapter 37.

keyFigures.name: Elihu
keyFigures.role: Says God uses affliction to teach and points to the rain.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: The one Elihu is answering.

keyThemes.explanation: God opens the ears of the afflicted.
Elihu warns Job not to choose sin over suffering.
We cannot fully know God or count his years.

Job 37.summary: Elihu's heart trembles at God's voice in the thunder and lightning (Job 37:1–5). God sends snow and rain, frost and whirlwind, as he wills (Job 37:6–13). He tells Job, "stand still, and consider the wondrous works of God" (Job 37:14–20). He ends, "Touching the Almighty, we cannot find him out" (Job 37:21–24).
Job 37.whereWeAre: Elihu began describing God's power in the storm in chapter 36. Now he describes thunder, snow, and the whirlwind and tells Job to "stand still, and consider the wondrous works of God" (Job 37:14). In chapter 38 God himself speaks.

keyFigures.name: Elihu
keyFigures.role: Describes God's power in the storm.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Told to stand still and consider God's works.

keyThemes.explanation: Thunder and lightning show God's power.
Elihu tells Job to stand still and think on God's wonders.
No one can find out the Almighty.

Job 38.summary: "Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind," telling him to gird up his loins and answer (Job 38:1–3). He asks, "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?" when "the morning stars sang together" (Job 38:4–7). He asks who shut up the sea and who commands the morning (Job 38:8–15). He asks whether Job has seen the gates of death or the treasures of the snow (Job 38:16–30). He asks whether Job can bind the Pleiades or feed the lions and ravens (Job 38:31–41).
Job 38.whereWeAre: Elihu finished speaking in chapter 37 as a storm gathered. Now "the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind" (Job 38:1), asking where Job was when he laid the foundations of the earth. Chapter 39 turns to the wild animals.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Answers Job out of the whirlwind with questions about creation.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Asked to answer God like a man.

keyThemes.explanation: God answers Job at last, out of the whirlwind.
God asks where Job was when the earth was made.
God sends the rain and feeds the lions and ravens.

Job 39.summary: God asks whether Job knows when the wild goats give birth (Job 39:1–4). He asks who set the wild ass free and whether the unicorn will serve him (Job 39:5–12). He describes the ostrich, which leaves her eggs in the earth because God has deprived her of wisdom (Job 39:13–18). He describes the war horse that "saith among the trumpets, Ha, ha" (Job 39:19–25). He asks whether the hawk and the eagle fly by Job's wisdom (Job 39:26–30).
Job 39.whereWeAre: God asked Job about the earth, the sea, and the stars in chapter 38. Now he asks about wild goats, the wild ass, the ostrich, the warhorse, and the eagle. In chapter 40 God calls on Job to answer.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Asks Job about the wild animals.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: The one God is questioning.

keyThemes.explanation: God cares for animals that people never tame.
The war horse's strength is a gift from God.
The hawk and the eagle do not fly by Job's wisdom.

Job 40.summary: God asks, "Shall he that contendeth with the Almighty instruct him?" (Job 40:1–2). Job answers, "Behold, I am vile... I will lay mine hand upon my mouth" (Job 40:3–5). God speaks again from the whirlwind: "Wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous?" (Job 40:6–9). He tells Job to humble every proud one if he can (Job 40:10–14). He describes behemoth, whose bones are like bars of iron (Job 40:15–24).
Job 40.whereWeAre: God showed Job the wild animals in chapter 39. Now Job puts his hand over his mouth, and God speaks again, asking whether Job can rule like God and describing behemoth. Chapter 41 describes leviathan.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Challenges Job and describes behemoth.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Lays his hand on his mouth.

keyThemes.explanation: Job lays his hand on his mouth.
God asks whether Job would make God wrong to make himself right.
Behemoth shows the might of what God made.

Job 41.summary: God asks, "Canst thou draw out leviathan with an hook?" (Job 41:1–9). No one dares stir him up, so who can stand before God (Job 41:10–11)? God describes leviathan's scales, his fiery breath, and his strong heart (Job 41:12–24). Swords, spears, and arrows cannot harm him, and "he is a king over all the children of pride" (Job 41:25–34).
Job 41.whereWeAre: God described behemoth in chapter 40. Now he describes leviathan, a creature no man can tame, and asks who then can stand before its Maker. In chapter 42 Job answers.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Describes leviathan, whom no one can tame.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: The one God is questioning.

keyThemes.explanation: No one can catch or tame leviathan.
If no one dares stir leviathan, no one can stand against God.
Leviathan is king over all the proud.

Job 42.summary: Job says to the LORD, "I know that thou canst do every thing," and admits he spoke of things too wonderful for him (Job 42:1–3). "I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee," he says, and he repents in dust and ashes (Job 42:4–6). The LORD tells Eliphaz that the friends have not spoken of him "the thing that is right," and Job prays for them (Job 42:7–9). The LORD gives Job twice as much as he had before, and his family comes to comfort him (Job 42:10–11). Job has seven sons and three daughters and lives 140 more years, dying "old and full of days" (Job 42:12–17).
Job 42.whereWeAre: God finished speaking in chapter 41. Job repents in dust and ashes, God rebukes the three friends, and Job's fortunes are restored twice over. Psalms follows, the book of Israel's songs and prayers, beginning with the blessing of the righteous man.

keyFigures.name: Job
keyFigures.role: Repents, prays for his friends, and is restored.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Rebukes the friends and blesses Job's latter end.

keyFigures.name: Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar
keyFigures.role: Offer sacrifices as the LORD commands.

keyFigures.name: Job's family
keyFigures.role: Come to comfort Job and bring him gifts.

keyThemes.explanation: Job moves from hearing about God to seeing him.
God says the friends spoke wrongly and asks Job to pray for them.
God gives Job twice as much as before.
